title: Backport one commit to the release branch
summary: A fix landed on main but customers are on the release branch. Copy that one commit across, record where it came from, and understand why it gets a different sha.
mental_model: Cherry-pick takes a commit's diff and applies it somewhere else, then makes a new commit. Same change, different parent, therefore a different sha. It copies; it never moves.

commit.message: Fix timing attack in token comparison

steps.title: Find the fix and confirm the release lacks it
steps.why: main has three commits the release branch does not, but only one of them is the security fix. The others must not go along for the ride — that is the whole reason for cherry-picking rather than merging.
steps.expect: Three commits ahead, one of them the fix.

steps.title: Copy just that commit
steps.why: `-x` appends a '(cherry picked from commit ...)' line to the message. On a release branch this is close to mandatory: six months later it is the only record of where the change came from.
steps.expect: The fix applied, with a provenance line in the message.

verify.label: the fix is on the release branch
…with its origin recorded
verify.hint: use -x so the provenance is in the message

steps.title: Confirm nothing else came with it
steps.why: The experimental feature and the readme stayed on main. The release branch received exactly one change — a shipping surface you can describe in one sentence.

verify.label: the unrelated commits were not copied

steps.title: See that the sha differs
steps.why: Same diff, different parent and different commit date, so a different object. This is why `git branch --contains` will not list the release branch for the original commit — identity and content are separate questions.
steps.expect: Two different shas; --contains lists only main.

steps.title: Prove the patches are equivalent
steps.why: `patch-id` hashes a diff, ignoring line numbers and commit metadata. Two commits with the same patch id are the same change — this is exactly how `git cherry` and rebase detect already-applied work.
commands: sh -c 'git show $(git log -1 --format=%H --grep="timing attack" main) | git patch-id'
steps.expect: The first hash matches on both lines; the commit shas after it differ.

steps.title: Tag the patch release
steps.why: A cherry-picked fix is only useful once it ships. The tag makes it namable, and `git describe` on the release branch now reports a clean version.
commands: git tag -a v3.2.1 -m "Patch release 3.2.1 — security fix"

steps.title: Audit the backport
steps.why: `git cherry` compares by patch id, so it correctly reports the fix as already present on the release branch despite the different sha. This is the command for 'what still needs backporting'.
steps.expect: The fix shown as '-' (present on both); the release-cut commit as '+'.

verify.label: the backport records where it came from
the fixed code is on the release branch
no unrelated work was dragged along
verify.hint: that is the difference between cherry-pick and merge

pitfalls: Always use `-x` when backporting. Without it there is no link back to the original commit and no way to audit what shipped where.
Cherry-picking a commit that depends on an earlier one produces a conflict or, worse, code that applies cleanly and is subtly wrong.
`git branch --contains` will not show the backport, because the sha differs. Use `git cherry` or `git log --grep` instead.
Repeatedly cherry-picking between long-lived branches is a sign the branches should be merged instead.
cheatsheet: copy a commit onto the current branch
